newsitem.title: USA: Medical groups urge U.S. train fewer doctors.
newsitem.headline: Medical groups urge U.S. train fewer doctors.

text.p: Key U.S. medical groups urged Congress on Friday to finance the training of fewer doctors to head off what they called a looming oversupply of physicians.
Six national associations said public funds should no longer be used to support the training of foreign medical school graduates but denied they were targeting foreign doctors.
"To decrease the rate of physician supply, limits must be placed on the number of medical school graduates entering graduate medical education," they said in a consensus statement.

In recent years, graduates of foreign medical schools, including U.S. citizens, have accounted for about 40 percent of those filling residency slots, the second phase of preparation for becoming a doctor.

The American Medical Association and the other groups said Congress should curb federal funding of residency slots, aligning their number "more closely" with the 17,000 or so graduates of the 142 U.S. medical schools. Currently, about 8,000 graduates of foreign medical schools join their U.S.-educated colleagues in filling the more than 25,000 openings available each year.

"And here is where the problem is," Dr. Jordan Cohen, president of the Association of American Colleges, said. "We recommend that federal support for residency training be reduced but that the number of funded positions be sufficient to provide opportunities for all U.S. graduates."

Cohen, at a news conference along with representatives of the other groups, said the predicted oversupply of doctors in the United States threatened to "diminish the attractiveness" of the profession to the most gifted U.S. students.
If the groups' recommendations were adopted, foreign nationals would remain welcome in the United States to train but would be obligated to return home to practice medicine.
Cohen, saying he was shattering a myth, said graduates of foreign medical schools were not more likely than graduates of U.S. schools to settle in underserved rural areas.

"In any event, given the projected large surplus of physicians, it makes no sense from a public policy point of view for this country to rely on another country's graduates to do this job. We must, and we can, find ways to resolve the problem of medically underserved Americans with our own graduates."
Critics of such proposals have said that many U.S. inner city hospitals that serve poor people depend heavily on their foreign-born residents.

The other organisations that endorsed the consensus statement were the American Association of Colleges of Osteopathic Medicine, the American Osteopathic Association, the Association of Academic Health Centres and the National Medical Association.
